title: IF YOU DON'T SPEAK IN TONGUES, DO YOU REALLY HAVE THE HOLY SPIRIT? THE BIBLICAL TRUTH THAT COULD SET THOUSANDS OF CHRISTIANS FREE
paragraphs: IF YOU DON'T SPEAK IN TONGUES, DO YOU REALLY HAVE THE HOLY SPIRIT? THE BIBLICAL TRUTH THAT COULD SET THOUSANDS OF CHRISTIANS FREE

Some believers have spent years wondering whether something is missing from their salvation because they have never spoken in tongues. But what if the very Scriptures being used to make them question their faith reveal a truth far more beautiful, far more challenging, and far more centered on Jesus Christ?
There is a kind of pain that happens inside a church that nobody talks about.
It happens when everyone around you seems to be experiencing something you have never experienced.
Hands are raised. Tears are falling. People are praying in languages you cannot understand. Someone begins to speak in tongues, and the atmosphere feels overwhelming.
Then a preacher says something that quietly breaks your heart.
"If you have truly received the Holy Spirit, you will speak in tongues."
And suddenly, the question is no longer about a spiritual gift.
It becomes a question about your salvation.

You love Jesus. You believe He died for your sins. You have confessed Him as Lord. You have cried over your failures, begged Him for forgiveness, and watched Him change things inside you that nobody else could change.
But you have never spoken in tongues.
So you go home wondering.
Is there something wrong with me?
Did God give everyone else something He refused to give me?
Am I really saved?
Does the Holy Spirit actually live inside me?
And perhaps the most painful question of all:
What if Jesus has accepted everyone in that room except me?
If you have ever wrestled with those thoughts, please do not leave this article halfway through.

Because we are going to open the Scriptures, examine the original Greek, confront some deeply misunderstood passages, and discover something that could change the way you understand the Holy Spirit for the rest of your life.
But first, we need to establish something important.
The question is not whether speaking in tongues is biblical. It is. The question is whether God requires every Christian to speak in tongues as proof of salvation or possession of the Holy Spirit.
Those are two very different questions.
And confusing them has wounded more sincere believers than many people realize.
The Bible does not invite us to deny what the Holy Spirit does. Neither does it give us permission to demand from every believer what the Spirit has not promised to give to every believer.
Jesus deserves better than either extreme.
And so do the people He purchased with His blood.
In Acts chapter 2, something extraordinary happened.

The disciples were gathered in Jerusalem when the Holy Spirit came upon them. There was a sound like a rushing mighty wind, tongues resembling fire appeared, and they began speaking in other tongues as the Spirit enabled them.
Acts 2:4 records:
"And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance." (KJV)
The Greek expression translated "other tongues" is ἑτέραις γλώσσαις (heterais glōssais).
The word heterais means "other" or "different," while glōssais means "tongues" or "languages."
But here is what we must not overlook.
The people listening understood what was being spoken.
Acts 2:8 records their astonishment:
"And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?" (KJV)
They were hearing the mighty works of God proclaimed in their own native languages.
This was not a performance.
It was not a competition over who was more spiritual.
It was not a demonstration that one group of Christians was superior to another.
It was a miraculous sign accompanying the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, bearing witness to God's mighty works and the unfolding mission of the Gospel.
People from different nations heard the message.
And Peter stood up to explain what was happening.
He pointed to the prophecy of Joel, announcing that God was pouring out His Spirit.
Sons and daughters would prophesy. Young men would see visions. Old men would dream dreams.
The promise was astonishing.
God was making His Spirit known among His people in a new-covenant fullness.
But notice something.
Peter did not end his sermon by saying, "Every person must now speak in tongues to be saved."
He proclaimed Jesus Christ.
His crucifixion.
His resurrection.
His exaltation.
And when the people were pierced to the heart, Peter called them to repentance and baptism in the name of Jesus Christ, with the promise of the gift of the Holy Spirit (Acts 2:38).
The center of Pentecost was not a spiritual experience detached from Christ.
The center of Pentecost was the risen and exalted Jesus pouring out the promised Holy Spirit.
And that distinction matters enormously.
Because whenever a spiritual gift becomes more important to us than the Savior who gives it, something has gone terribly wrong.
Now someone may understandably object.
"But what about the other passages in Acts where people received the Holy Spirit and spoke in tongues?"
That is a fair question.
And it deserves a fair answer.

In Acts 10, the Holy Spirit fell upon Cornelius and those listening to Peter. Jewish believers were astonished that the gift of the Spirit had been poured out upon Gentiles, because they heard them speaking in tongues and magnifying God.

In Acts 19, Paul encountered disciples in Ephesus. After they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus and Paul laid hands on them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied.
These events are real.
They are inspired Scripture.
They must never be explained away simply because they challenge someone's theology.
But here is the crucial question:
Does the fact that something happened to certain believers mean Scripture commands that it must happen to every believer?
That is where careful Bible interpretation becomes essential.
The book of Acts records significant moments in the Gospel's expansion, including the Spirit's coming upon Jews, Samaritans, Gentiles, and other disciples.
These events demonstrate that the risen Christ was gathering people into His church across boundaries that had once divided them.
Yet Acts does not record tongues accompanying every conversion.
When the Samaritans received the Holy Spirit in Acts 8, the text reports that Simon saw something remarkable, but it does not explicitly identify that manifestation as speaking in tongues.
When the Ethiopian official believed and was baptized in Acts 8, no speaking in tongues is reported.
When Lydia's heart was opened to respond to Paul's message in Acts 16, no speaking in tongues is reported.
When the Philippian jailer believed in the Lord Jesus, no speaking in tongues is reported.
This does not prove those believers never spoke in tongues later.
But it does mean we cannot honestly claim that Acts explicitly presents tongues as the recorded experience of every convert.
And then we arrive at a passage that every Christian discussing this subject must face.
First Corinthians chapter 12.
Paul is writing to a church deeply familiar with spiritual gifts.
In fact, the Corinthians were so fascinated with spiritual manifestations that they needed correction concerning pride, disorder, division, and love.
Paul does not tell them to despise spiritual gifts.
He teaches them how to understand those gifts in the body of Christ.
First Corinthians 12:4 says:
"Now there are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit." (KJV)
The Greek word translated "gifts" is χαρισμάτων (charismatōn), the plural form of charisma.
It refers to gracious gifts.
The word is connected to χάρις (charis), meaning grace or favor.
That connection is beautiful.
Spiritual gifts are not trophies awarded to people who have become spiritually impressive.
They are gifts of grace.
You do not earn grace.
You receive it.
And the Holy Spirit distributes gifts according to His will.
First Corinthians 12:11 states that the one Spirit distributes to each person individually as He wills.
Not as the congregation demands.
Not as a preacher insists.
Not as someone's insecurity dictates.
As the Spirit wills.
Paul then describes the church as a body.
Different members.
Different functions.
One Lord.
One Spirit.
One body.
And then he asks a series of questions.
First Corinthians 12:29–30:
"Are all apostles? are all prophets? are all teachers? are all workers of miracles?
Have all the gifts of healing? do all speak with tongues? do all interpret?" (KJV)
Read that again.
"Do all speak with tongues?"
In the Greek text, the question appears as:
μὴ πάντες γλώσσαις λαλοῦσιν;
Mē pantes glōssais lalousin?
The word μή (mē) introduces a question that expects a negative answer in this construction.
The phrase asks, in effect:
"Surely not everyone speaks in tongues, do they?"
The expected answer is:
No.
Not all are apostles.
Not all are prophets.
Not all are teachers.
Not all perform miracles.
Not all have gifts of healing.
And not all speak in tongues.
This is not an obscure theological argument built on one isolated English translation.
It is the natural force of Paul's rhetorical questions in their Greek context.
And it changes the conversation.
Because if the apostle Paul explicitly teaches that not everyone speaks in tongues, we must be extremely careful before telling someone that every genuine Christian must speak in tongues.

Some Pentecostal theologians distinguish between tongues as an initial sign of Spirit baptism and tongues as an ongoing congregational gift. Within that interpretation, they understand Paul's question in 1 Corinthians 12:30 to concern the public gift rather than every instance of tongues.
That distinction deserves to be represented fairly.
But it also needs to be recognized as a theological interpretation that must be argued from Scripture, not simply assumed.
The New Testament does not explicitly state in a universal command that every Christian must speak in tongues to prove salvation.
And Paul's teaching about the Spirit's distribution of gifts gives serious reason to reject making one particular gift a universal measure of Christian authenticity.
Now imagine the relief that truth could bring to someone who has spent twenty years wondering whether God has rejected them.
A mother who prays over her children every night.
A father who quietly fights temptation because he wants to honor Christ.
A young believer who opens a Bible in secret because the people around him mock his faith.
A widow who whispers, "Jesus, help me," when grief becomes unbearable.
A former addict who has turned away from destruction and now clings to the mercy of God.
None of these people should be told that their faith is counterfeit merely because they have never spoken in tongues.
But we must go even deeper.
Because the greatest question is not simply whether every believer speaks in tongues.
It is this:
How does Scripture tell us that someone belongs to Jesus Christ?
Romans 8:9 gives a sobering answer:
"Now if any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his." (KJV)
The Holy Spirit is not an optional addition to genuine Christian life.
Every person who truly belongs to Christ has the Spirit of Christ.
And Paul makes an equally important statement in Ephesians 1:13.
Speaking to believers, he says that after hearing the word of truth, the Gospel of their salvation, and believing in Christ, they were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit.
The Greek word translated "sealed" is ἐσφραγίσθητε (esphragisthēte).
It comes from the verb sphragizō, meaning to seal or mark with a seal.
In the ancient world, a seal could communicate ownership, authenticity, or authority.
Paul uses this imagery to describe God's gracious action toward those who belong to Christ.
Notice what the passage identifies.
They heard the Gospel.
They believed in Christ.
They were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit.
Paul does not add, "Provided they all subsequently spoke in tongues."
He directs attention to faith in Jesus and God's action through the Spirit.
First Corinthians 12:13 also declares that in one Spirit believers were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, slaves or free, and were all made to drink of one Spirit.
Christians differ in how they understand the relationship between this passage and later experiences of empowerment by the Holy Spirit.
Those discussions are worth having.
But the central truth remains.
No genuine believer is spiritually abandoned by Christ simply because that believer lacks a particular spiritual gift.
And that leads us to one of the most searching passages in the entire discussion.
First Corinthians chapter 13.
Paul writes:
The word translated "charity" is ἀγάπη (agapē).
Love.
Paul's language is deliberately striking.
Even the most extraordinary speech, without love, amounts to empty noise.
Think about that.
A person could possess an astonishing spiritual gift and still be acting without the very love that should characterize the followers of Jesus.
That should humble every one of us.
Those who speak in tongues should never boast as though the gift makes them superior.
Those who do not speak in tongues should never mock, despise, or automatically dismiss those who do.
Paul himself said:
"I thank my God, I speak with tongues more than ye all." (1 Corinthians 14:18, KJV)
He also said:
"Wherefore, brethren, covet to prophesy, and forbid not to speak with tongues." (1 Corinthians 14:39, KJV)
That is important.
The biblical answer is not to reject speaking in tongues.
The biblical answer is to put it in its proper place.
Paul valued the gift, while insisting that its use in gathered worship must serve the church through intelligibility, interpretation, order, and edification.

In 1 Corinthians 14:5, he even expressed his desire that the Corinthians speak in tongues, while emphasizing the greater congregational benefit of intelligible prophecy unless tongues are interpreted.
And in 1 Corinthians 14:27–28, he gave instructions about orderly public use and the necessity of interpretation.
The New Testament therefore gives us neither permission to manufacture spiritual experiences nor permission to ridicule gifts of the Holy Spirit.
It calls us to pursue love, desire spiritual gifts, test what is taught, and build up the church.
There is another question people often ask.
"Are biblical tongues always recognizable human languages?"
Acts 2 clearly describes hearers recognizing their native languages.
First Corinthians 12–14, however, discusses speech that may not be understood by others present unless interpreted. Paul also uses the expression "tongues of men and of angels" in 1 Corinthians 13:1.
Christians disagree over whether that latter expression establishes an actual category of angelic speech or functions as part of Paul's rhetorical emphasis.
We should not pretend that every detail is beyond debate.
What Scripture clearly teaches is that the Holy Spirit is sovereign, the church must be edified, and spiritual gifts must never become a substitute for love and obedience.
And please hear this.
The Holy Spirit is not given to make us obsessed with proving that we are more spiritual than the person sitting beside us.
He glorifies Jesus Christ.
Jesus Himself said in John 16:14:
"He shall glorify me: for he shall receive of mine, and shall shew it unto you." (KJV)
That is the direction of the Spirit's ministry.
Toward Christ.
Toward truth.
Toward holiness.
Toward the glory of the Son.
This is where the question becomes painfully personal.
Because some Christians have been so consumed with obtaining one manifestation that they have neglected the transformation the Holy Spirit is producing in their daily lives.
They want a supernatural experience, but refuse to forgive their spouse.
They want a public display of power, but continue to deceive people in private.
They want to sound spiritual in church, but will not repent of bitterness, cruelty, dishonesty, or pride.
And we need to be careful here.
Speaking in tongues does not prove that someone is living in rebellion.
Neither does the absence of tongues prove that someone is spiritually mature.
But spiritual experiences cannot replace repentance.
Jesus warned in Matthew 7:22–23 that people could appeal to extraordinary works done in His name and yet be exposed as workers of lawlessness.
That warning should shake us.
Because it is possible to be fascinated by spiritual power while resisting the Lordship of Jesus.
And it is possible to appear unimpressive to the world while living a life of deep, genuine faith.
Galatians 5:22–23 describes the fruit of the Spirit:
Love.
Joy.
Peace.
Longsuffering.
Gentleness.
Goodness.
Faithfulness.
Meekness.
Self-control.
The Greek word translated "fruit" is καρπός (karpos).
It points to the produce or result of the Spirit's work.
And while fruit must never be confused with a means of earning salvation, it does reveal something about the transforming work of God.
A person may speak eloquently about spiritual power while remaining unwilling to love.
Another person may never speak in tongues but show remarkable patience, mercy, self-control, and faithfulness under suffering.
Which life is demonstrating the character of Christ?
That question deserves more attention than it often receives.
Because the ultimate goal of Christian discipleship is not to make everyone display the same spiritual gift.
It is to make disciples who increasingly resemble Jesus.
And perhaps you are reading this with a different wound.
Perhaps you have spoken in tongues for years.
You know the experience is real to you.
You have prayed, worshiped, and sought God with sincere devotion.
But now you feel as though this article is challenging something precious in your walk with Christ.
Please understand.
You are not the enemy.
Your spiritual experience does not need to be mocked for Scripture to be examined honestly.
And the gift you believe God has given you does not need to be denied for us to acknowledge that other believers may receive different gifts.
The church does not need another battle in which Christians tear each other apart over the very Spirit who unites them in Christ.
We need humility.
We need discernment.
We need biblical conviction without spiritual arrogance.
And we need the courage to admit when a tradition has gone further than the written Word.
Because no denomination, ministry, preacher, or spiritual movement has authority to add a requirement for salvation that the Gospel itself does not establish.
Not even Gospel Warrior.
Every teaching must bow before Scripture.
Every spiritual experience must be tested by truth.
And every Christian must ultimately answer to Jesus Christ.
Now let us address one more passage that frequently enters this discussion.
Mark 16:17 says:
"And these signs shall follow them that believe; In my name shall they cast out devils; they shall speak with new tongues." (KJV)
This verse appears in the longer ending of Mark, verses 9–20.

An important textual fact must be acknowledged: some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts of Mark do not contain this longer ending, and modern Bible editions commonly note the manuscript issue.
Christians hold different views about its originality and canonical status.
Even among those who receive the longer ending as Scripture, the passage does not necessarily require that every individual believer personally demonstrate every sign mentioned.
The same context refers to other extraordinary signs.
We must be consistent in our interpretation rather than selecting one sign and declaring it universally mandatory while treating the others differently.
The central doctrine of salvation and the Spirit's presence in believers should be established from the broader and clearer teaching of the New Testament.
And that broader teaching continually brings us back to Jesus.
Not our performance.
Not our spiritual vocabulary.
Not our ability to reproduce someone else's experience.
Jesus.
The crucified Savior.
The risen Lord.
The One who receives sinners who come to Him in repentance and faith.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares:
"For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Not of works, lest any man should boast." (KJV)
The Greek word for grace is χάρις (charis).
The word for faith is πίστις (pistis).
And the Gospel announces that salvation is God's gracious gift, received through faith, not a reward for human achievement.
No spiritual gift can purchase forgiveness.
No religious performance can erase sin.
No supernatural experience can replace the blood of Jesus Christ.
Only Christ saves.
Only Christ reconciles sinners to God.
Only Christ bore our sins and rose again.
And only Christ is worthy of our ultimate confidence.
Perhaps that is what someone desperately needs to hear today.
You have been trying so hard to prove that you belong to God.
You have attended every prayer meeting.
You have stood in every altar line.
You have asked people to lay hands on you.
You have whispered syllables because you were afraid that silence meant failure.
You have watched others weep with joy while you quietly wondered why heaven seemed silent toward you.
And somewhere along the way, you began measuring God's love by an experience you could not produce.
But listen carefully.
You cannot manufacture the Holy Spirit's gifts, and you do not have to manufacture evidence to persuade Jesus to love those who are His.
That does not mean you should stop seeking God.
It means you should seek Him truthfully.
Ask Him to fill you with wisdom.
Ask Him to strengthen your witness.
Ask Him to deepen your prayer life.
Ask Him to make you holy.
Ask Him to use you for the good of His church.
And yes, you may humbly ask Him for spiritual gifts, including tongues, while submitting to His wisdom and will.
But never let another person's gift become the judge of your salvation.
And never let your own spiritual experience become a throne from which you look down on another child of God.
There is room at the foot of the cross for the believer who speaks in tongues and the believer who does not.
Both must repent.
Both need grace.
Both must depend upon Jesus.
Both need the sanctifying work of the Holy Spirit.
Both are called to love one another.
And neither has the right to boast.
Because the ground beneath the cross is level.
Now perhaps someone will say:
"But shouldn't Christians desire more of the Holy Spirit?"
Absolutely.
We should hunger for deeper fellowship with God, greater obedience, stronger faith, and the Spirit's empowering work.
Ephesians 5:18 calls believers to be filled with the Spirit.
The Greek command πληροῦσθε ἐν πνεύματι (plērousthe en pneumati) carries the force of an ongoing command to be filled with the Spirit.
This is not an invitation to spiritual complacency.
It is a call to a life continually shaped by God's presence and power.
But notice the surrounding context.
Paul speaks of worship, thanksgiving, and relationships marked by reverence for Christ.
The Spirit-filled life is not reduced to a single outward manifestation.
It reaches into how we worship.
How we speak.
How we treat people.
How we forgive.
How we endure.
How we obey.
And how we glorify Jesus when nobody is watching.
There is a profound difference between wanting the Holy Spirit to transform your life and wanting a spiritual experience merely to silence your insecurity.
God calls us to the first.
And His grace can free us from the second.
Maybe the deepest issue in this entire conversation is not tongues at all.
Maybe it is our tendency to turn the Christian life into another system of comparison.
Who prays longer?
Who worships louder?
Who has the most dramatic testimony?
Who has the most impressive gift?
Who has the greatest platform?
Who looks the most anointed?
And while we compare ourselves, someone in the back of the church is quietly drowning in shame.
Someone who genuinely loves Jesus is afraid to admit that they have never experienced what everyone else seems to celebrate.
Someone who is fighting to remain faithful is beginning to believe they are a second-class Christian.
That is why this discussion matters.
Because truth is not merely about winning a theological argument.
Truth can protect a wounded conscience.
Truth can expose spiritual pride.
Truth can correct a harmful teaching.
Truth can restore the attention of a frightened believer to the Savior who never asked them to earn His mercy.
But there is also a warning for those who have never spoken in tongues.
Do not use this article as an excuse to become cynical toward the supernatural work of God.
Do not confuse discernment with unbelief.
Do not ridicule sincere believers simply because their experiences differ from yours.
Scripture commands us not to quench the Spirit (1 Thessalonians 5:19), and also to test everything and hold fast to what is good (1 Thessalonians 5:21).
We need both.
Openness without discernment can lead to deception.
Discernment without humility can harden into pride.
But biblical discernment, exercised in love, leads us back to the truth of Christ.
And here is where our Gospel Warrior message becomes more than a slogan.
The scandal is not that one Christian speaks in tongues and another does not.
The deeper scandal is that sinful human beings, rescued by mercy, can still find ways to turn God's gracious gifts into instruments of comparison, exclusion, and pride.
We take what was meant to serve the body and use it to divide the body.
We take what was meant to glorify Christ and use it to glorify ourselves.
We take the language of the Spirit and sometimes forget the character of the Savior.
But grace calls us back.
Back to the cross.
Back to repentance.
Back to humility.
Back to the truth that the Holy Spirit does not exist to make Jesus compete with our religious experiences.
The Spirit glorifies Jesus.
And Jesus is enough.
Not because spiritual gifts are unimportant.
But because spiritual gifts are never greater than the One who gives them.
If you speak in tongues, use whatever gift God has entrusted to you with humility, love, biblical order, and a sincere desire to build up His people.
If you do not speak in tongues, do not assume that God has abandoned you.
Look to Christ.
Examine whether you truly believe the Gospel.
Turn from sin.
Walk in obedience.
Remain in His Word.
Seek the Spirit's work in your life.
And remember that your standing before God rests on the saving work of Jesus Christ, not on your ability to produce a particular manifestation.
If you have never repented and placed your trust in Jesus, this is not an invitation merely to feel better about yourself.
It is an invitation to come to the Savior.
Confess your sin.
Believe that Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose from the dead.
Turn to Him in faith.
Receive His mercy.
And follow Him as Lord.
Romans 10:9 calls us to confess Jesus as Lord and believe that God raised Him from the dead.
The Gospel is not, "Speak in tongues and you will be saved."
The Gospel is the good news of Jesus Christ, crucified and risen, who saves those who come to Him in faith.
And that is the truth no spiritual pressure should ever be allowed to bury.
Have you ever felt spiritually inferior because you could not speak in tongues?
Have you ever been told that your relationship with God was incomplete because you had not experienced what someone else experienced?
Or perhaps you have spoken in tongues and have a testimony of how God has used that gift to deepen your prayer life and strengthen your faith.
There is room for your voice here too.
And if you believe God has genuinely given you the gift of tongues, share your testimony with humility and biblical reflection.
Let this comment section become a place where people listen, learn, encourage one another, and point each other back to Jesus.
Not a battlefield.
Not a competition.
A place for truth spoken in love.
Because someone reading your testimony may be closer to giving up than you realize.
And your words may remind them to open their Bible, seek the Lord, and remain faithful.
Not simply because you agree with every sentence, but because this is a question that deserves serious, Scripture-centered conversation.
Somewhere there may be a Christian who has become proud of a spiritual gift and needs a gentle reminder that love matters more than spiritual status.
Somewhere there may be an unbeliever who has watched Christians argue over spiritual experiences without ever clearly hearing the Gospel of grace.
Let them encounter the truth about Jesus.
Because discipleship is not meant to end when an emotional article ends.
It should continue into prayer, Scripture, fellowship, repentance, obedience, and daily growth in Christ.
These resources are intended to help believers study the Bible more deeply, grow in spiritual maturity, strengthen their faith, and continue learning long after they finish reading a Facebook post.
And if this ministry has helped you, I want to invite you to consider something more personal.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that each person should give according to what they have decided in their heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
That means no pressure.
No guilt.
And no promise that financial support will purchase spiritual favor.
If you are able and freely willing to help, your generosity can make a real difference in sustaining this work.
You can glorify God through faithful service, prayer, generosity, and sharing the truth of His Word in many ways.
Those products are simply an expression of appreciation. They are not the reason we preach Christ.
Bigger than a social media page.
It is about helping people encounter the truth of Scripture and grow as disciples of Jesus.
If you believe this work is worth sustaining, and you are in a position to help, I warmly invite you to become part of the community that supports it.
We will stand before the Lord who knows every heart.
The Lord who sees beyond appearances.
The Lord who cannot be impressed by religious performance.
The Lord whose grace is our only hope.
And when that day comes, the most important question will not be whether you managed to sound like the most spiritual person in the room.
It will be whether you truly belong to Jesus Christ.

So if you have spent years feeling rejected because you have never spoken in tongues, I pray that Scripture has helped you see the difference between a gracious spiritual gift and the saving grace of God.
And if you have been blessed with that gift, I pray you will use it in a way that makes people marvel not at you, but at the Savior you serve.
May those who have been wounded find healing.
May those who have become proud find humility.
May those who have been confused find clarity.
May those who have become divided rediscover the love of Christ.
And may those who do not yet know Jesus discover that salvation is not found in religious performance, but in the crucified and risen Son of God.
Because the Holy Spirit's greatest purpose is not to make us famous for our experiences.
It is to glorify Jesus Christ.
And if your voice has never spoken in tongues, that does not mean your name is missing from the heart of the Savior who died to redeem you.
